name: Gym and loud lifting for voice
lead: 'Gym and loud lifting for voice' is the belief that weight training, and in particular grunting or shouting while lifting, can give a deeper, more resonant voice. For people working on how they come across, a deeper voice is part of a more masculine, authoritative presence, and lifting is one of the routines they try for it.

Reference sources describe adult speaking pitch as typically about 90 to 155 Hz in men and 165 to 255 Hz in women [1]. Wikipedia's puberty article says androgens drive larynx growth, with the longer, thicker vocal folds lowering the fundamental frequency by roughly an octave in boys, usually gradually [3]. That is the biological route proponents point to when they link training, testosterone and voice.

Research on adult voice pitch and hormones comes from testosterone treatment trials. A 2015 trial in 71 women given weekly testosterone injections for 24 weeks reported dose-dependent drops in average vocal pitch tied to rising free testosterone [4]. These were pharmacological doses, and no published study located has tested whether lifting or grunting changes adult voice pitch. Voice therapy, as practiced by speech-language pathologists, targets vocal fold closure, pitch, volume and quality, and its hygienic approach advises avoiding phonotraumatic behaviours such as yelling [2].

paras: Proponents link strength training with higher testosterone or a more resonant 'chest' voice, and treat loud exertion noises as vocal practice. These beliefs are anecdotal; a coaching literature repeats them without controlled studies. Gym culture itself notes the sounds of lifting: a T Nation member describes a gym attendant adding mats beneath a bar because she disliked the noises of men lifting, and another thread describes a gym threatening to remove heavy weights over noise [5][6].

Androgens drive laryngeal growth in puberty and lower voice pitch by roughly an octave in males [3]. In adults, the best-studied effect is from testosterone treatment: in a 2015 Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism trial, women on 12.5 mg and 25 mg weekly injections had significantly lower average pitch on a sustained vowel than placebo, and the change tracked free testosterone levels; participants did not necessarily notice voice changes [4]. No trial has measured voice pitch in lifters.

Voice therapy literature describes shouting, cheering and similar forceful phonation as behaviors to reduce, because they can traumatize the vocal folds.[2] Resonant voice approaches aim to lower the force of vocal fold collision.[2] The exercises in therapy are vocal rather than physical-fitness exercises.[2]
Resonant voice approaches aim to produce a strong voice with lower vocal fold collision force [2].
No studies found on lifting or grunting and adult voice pitch. Related research: a 2015 trial of testosterone injections in women reported dose-dependent decreases in average pitch [4].

lore.intro: The idea appears in voice-related corners of appearance culture as a hopeful link between strength, testosterone and voice, and gym noise is a recurring theme on lifting forums.

claims.claim: Lifting weights deepens the voice by raising testosterone.
claims.believers: Proponents say strength training raises testosterone and builds a fuller chest voice.
claims.experts: Androgens lower pitch in puberty [3], and high-dose testosterone lowered pitch in a 2015 trial in women [4]; no study has tested lifting itself.

claims.claim: Grunting and shouting during lifts trains a deeper voice.
claims.believers: Believers treat loud exertion noises as vocal practice.
claims.experts: Voice therapy guidance lists yelling and forceful phonation as behaviours to reduce because they can traumatise the vocal folds [2].

card.summary: Folk belief that grunting while lifting deepens the voice; nothing has tested it.
card.note: Voice therapy sources list yelling as a behavior to avoid.

quick.overview:
This is a folk belief that lifting weights, especially while making loud sounds, lowers the voice.

No published study located has tested it, and the sources found are thin.
quick.mechanism: Believers point to strength training and testosterone or to loud vocalizing as practice. No tested mechanism exists.
quick.risks: Voice therapy guidance lists yelling and forceful phonation as phonotraumatic behaviors that hygiene approaches advise reducing.

chain: Strength training and loud, chest-driven exertion
Higher testosterone and more practised low-register phonation (as believed)
angle.text: Lifters who want a deeper voice train and vocalise in the gym in the belief that muscle, testosterone and chest resonance will lower pitch. Nothing has measured this in adults.
